essence: Visitors to Maurilia must admire old postcards of the provincial town and regret its changes politely, yet the postcard city was never this city's past: successive cities can occupy one site under one name while remaining strangers to each other.
textDetails: Visitors are asked to tour the city while also looking through old postcards of how it once looked.
The postcards show the identical square with a hen where the bus station now stands.
A bandstand where the overpass now is.
Two young ladies with white parasols where the munitions factory now is.
So as not to disappoint the inhabitants, the traveler has to praise the postcard city and say he prefers it to the present one.
His regret at the changes must stay within definite limits.
The splendour and wealth of the metropolis do not make up for a certain grace the old provincial town has lost.
That grace can be appreciated only now, in the postcards; when the provincial town was there to be seen, nobody saw anything graceful in it.
The metropolis offers one extra charm: what it has turned into lets people gaze back fondly at what it used to be.
The traveler should not tell them that distinct cities sometimes succeed each other on one site and under one name, each rising and dying without knowledge of or contact with the others.
Sometimes the inhabitants' names, the accent of their voices and even their facial features carry over unchanged.
Yet the gods who inhabit the space under names and over places have departed silently, and strangers have installed themselves in their stead (the Italian may mean foreign gods; unverified).
Asking whether the newcomers are better or worse than the old is futile, as nothing links the two.
So the postcards do not record Maurilia's past at all: they show another city that by chance bore the same name.
visualConcept: One square, two cities that never meet. By default we see the present metropolis on a card-like square plinth: grey concrete blocks of five to twelve storeys, a bus station with its canopy and idling buses on the north side of the square, a concrete overpass slicing along the east side on tall piers, and a munitions factory with sawtooth roofs and smoking chimneys in the south-west, all under a pearly industrial smog. Hovering above each of those three structures hangs a giant old postcard with a deckled white border, and through it, as through a window, you see the same spot in another city: a hen on the cobbles above the bus station, an octagonal bandstand above the overpass, two young ladies with white parasols above the factory, all in warm sepia with hand-tinted washes that glow against the grey. A dozen smaller postcards drift around the square, and at a postcard kiosk the visitor is shown cards by smiling hosts. The only things common to both cities are the name MAURILIA on a name board at the same spot, the outline of the square, and the inhabitants, whose figures and faces are identical in both. In the postcard city a few soft warm lights hover just beneath the name board and above the roofs, the gods who dwell under names and over places; in the metropolis they are gone, and colder, unfamiliar lights sit where they were. The conceit reads because the two cities share coordinates but not a single shape: the postcards are not the past of what lies beneath them, only another city that happened to bear the same name.
layout: Plan convention: +X east, -Z north, y up. Rounded-square plinth 36 x 36 (corner radius 6), top at y=0, 1.0 thick, its sides finished like the deckled edge of a card. Central square 14 x 10 with the same paving outline in both cities. Present metropolis: about 55 instanced blocks (footprints 2-5, heights 2-5.5) around the square, grey concrete with glass window grids; bus station on the north side of the square (canopy 6 x 3 at h 1.0 over 4 buses, each 1.2 long); overpass, a deck 1.6 wide at h 1.6 on 8 piers, curving about 28 units along the east side of the square from the north-east corner to the south edge, carrying streams of tiny cars; munitions factory in the south-west quarter (sawtooth shed 8 x 5, 1.2 high, two chimneys 6 high, perimeter fence); 16 sodium street lamps. Postcard kiosk on the west side of the square with a rack of cards, the traveler and two hosts. Name board reading MAURILIA (canvas texture, 3 x 0.5 on two posts, top at 1.5) at the square's north-west corner, same position in both cities. Hero postcards: 3 cards 2.6 x 1.7 hovering 1.5 above the bus station, the overpass and the factory, each a portal into the postcard city (render target from a matched camera into a hidden scene, or a stencil window; fallback, a still rendered once at load), plus 12 small cards (0.8 x 0.55) drifting at h 3-8. Postcard city (toggle): about 70 low houses (0.5-1.0 tall) with hipped tile roofs, 24 round-crowned trees, a cobbled square, an octagonal bandstand (r 1.2, 1.4 high, little pagoda roof) on the overpass site, a hen (0.07 tall) on the bus station site, two young ladies with white parasols (parasol r 0.12) on the factory site; 6 god-lights (soft warm spheres r 0.08) hovering between the name board and the rooftops. Inhabitants: 14 figures at the same coordinates and in the same colours in both cities.
signatureMotion: 1) The living present: buses slide in and out of the station, paired headlights and taillights stream along the overpass, slow smoke rises from the factory chimneys, postcards drift and turn like leaves, catching glints on their glossy faces, and the traveler turns a card in his hands. 2) Portals with parallax: as the camera orbits, the view inside each hero postcard shifts in true 3D, yet time there has almost stopped: the hen pecks once in a while, a parasol tilts, the bandstand's pennant stirs, with a faint sepia flicker like old film. 3) The discontinuous change (on toggle): nothing morphs into anything; the departing city sinks and dissolves into fog and dust (2.5 s), leaving only bare paving, the name board and the inhabitants; a beat of emptiness (1 s); then the other city rises in place (2.5 s). Leaving the postcard city, the god-lights drift up and away into the fog before the metropolis arrives, and they do not come back.
interactionDescription: Switches the whole site between today's metropolis and the provincial city of the postcards, with total discontinuity rather than a morph: one city vanishes completely before the other assembles. The name board, the outline of the square and the inhabitants stay exactly where they were, and nothing else carries over. In postcard mode the scene takes the postcard's grade (sepia toning, hand-tinted rose, sky and leaf washes, paper grain, a deckled vignette) and the god-lights hover beneath the name; returning to the present, they drift away into the fog without a sound, and colder, unfamiliar lights settle where they were.
mood: Present: a smog-veiled industrial afternoon, flat pearly-grey light with the sun a pale disc, the overpass and factory in cool shadow, sodium lamps already burning under the deck, while the postcards glow warm like windows onto sunlight. Postcard: a bright, soft summer morning frozen in sepia, still air, hand-tinted pastels. Polite nostalgia with an undertow of estrangement.
caption: In Maurilia the tour comes with old postcards: the very same square, a hen where buses now idle, a bandstand on the spot the overpass now spans, two young women shaded by white parasols where the munitions works smoke. Praise the lost grace and regret it, though only so much. Never tell your hosts that the cards show another city that merely wore this name, whose gods left in silence and let strangers move in.
motto: A name outlives every city that wears it.
camera: From the west-south-west at a gentle height: distance 40, elevation 30 deg, target (0, 2, 0) at the centre of the square; postcard kiosk and traveler in the foreground, the bus station and its postcard on the left, the overpass and its postcard across the back, the factory and its postcard front right, the name board front left. Slow orbit of +/-30 deg so the portal parallax inside the postcards is felt.
